The Irish pollan (Coregonus pollan) is a freshwater coregonid endemic to Lough Neagh and a handful of other Irish loughs, where it occupies a pelagic feeding niche similar to that of its Arctic charr and whitefish relatives. Field surveys of adult pollan indicate that individuals ultimately attain a maximum total length of 35 cm [Li = 35 cm], a value that places this species among the smaller-bodied members of the genus Coregonus. Data from gillnet samples and length-frequency distributions suggest that females reach puberty at a significantly smaller size, with a total length at puberty of 27 cm [Lp = 27 cm], a measurement derived from the length at which 50 percent of sampled females exhibited mature gonads. This difference between pubertal and asymptotic length reflects a life-history strategy in which continued somatic growth accompanies the onset of reproductive activity, a pattern common among iteroparous coregonids inhabiting relatively stable lacustrine environments.

The reproductive output of Irish pollan has not been measured directly in wild populations, but comparative data from the closely related species Coregonus chadary provide a useful proxy for estimating maximum fecundity. A gravid female of that species produces approximately 12,100 eggs per spawning event, and a comparable value is expected for pollan. When combined with a spawning frequency of one event per breeding season [F_R_i = one event per breeding season], the daily maximum reproductive rate can be inferred as roughly 5.5 eggs per day [Ri = roughly 5.5 eggs per day] under the typical thermal regime experienced during the spawning period, which occurs at a water temperature of 10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C]. This estimate assumes that all eggs are produced in a single annual event, consistent with the semelparous tendency of some northern coregonids, though pollan are better described as iteroparous with an extended reproductive lifespan.

Egg size in Coregonus pollan has been measured from preserved ovarian samples, with a mean egg diameter of approximately 1.5 millimeters. Using the formula for the volume of a sphere, this diameter corresponds to a wet weight at birth of 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], a value that reflects the considerable yolk investment characteristic of cold-water coregonids with relatively large, demersal eggs. Upon hatching, the yolk-sac larvae emerge at this modest mass and rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves for the first several weeks of life. The energetic cost of producing such large eggs is substantial, and fecundity is correspondingly limited; a single female may produce only a few thousand eggs annually, a trade-off that constrains population recruitment in years of poor zooplankton availability during the critical first-feeding period.

Body size at later life stages has been estimated using a length-weight relationship derived from empirical measurements of pollan captured across multiple seasons: wet weight scales isometrically with total length according to the equation 0.00537 times length raised to the 3.22 power. Applying this relationship to the asymptotic length of 35 cm yields an ultimate wet weight of 503 grams [Wwi = 503 grams], a mass that represents the maximum size attained by fully grown adults in Lough Neagh. Similarly, females reach 218 grams [Wwp = 218 grams] at puberty, a point that corresponds to just over 40 percent of their ultimate body mass, a relatively low threshold compared to some iteroparous salmonids, which typically delay reproduction until reaching at least 60 percent of asymptotic size.

Longevity data for Coregonus pollan come primarily from otolith-based age determinations conducted on individuals collected during commercial and research gillnet surveys. The oldest documented specimen in the Lough Neagh population reached an age of approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years] under the relatively cool thermal conditions characteristic of this deep lake, where summer water temperatures rarely exceed 10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C]. This lifespan is modest compared to that of Arctic charr, which can exceed 25 years in high-latitude systems, but is typical for coregonids occupying temperate lakes with moderate productivity. The combination of a decade-long lifespan with early maturation and modest adult body size positions the Irish pollan as a relatively fast-lived species within its genus, a demographic strategy that may buffer populations against the effects of variable juvenile survival in an unpredictable lacustrine environment.
